paraphrase: Those who wish soon to attain omniscience should, in brief, strive in three things: compassion, the awakening mind and practice.

paraphrase: Kamalaśīla explains the Laṅkāvatāra's verses as stages of meditation: the yogin first analyses form as nothing apart from mind, then examines mind itself and finds it without own-nature, then abandons even the image of non-duality, and abides in the imageless wisdom that sees the Mahāyāna.
notes: Section-level ref in the first Bhāvanākrama (local e-text asian_classics); paraphrase condensed.

paraphrase: Knowing that compassion alone is the root of all the qualities of buddhahood, one should cultivate it at the very beginning; and it is great compassion that causes the Buddhas not to abide in nirvāṇa but to remain for the good of the whole world.

paraphrase: Wisdom arising from hearing should first be produced, by which one grasps the meaning of scripture; then by wisdom arising from reflection one discerns the definitive and the provisional meaning; having ascertained it, one should cultivate what is real and not what is unreal, for otherwise, cultivating the mistaken and not removing doubt, correct knowledge will not arise.

paraphrase: In brief every concentration has six faults — laziness, forgetting the object, laxity and excitement, non-application and over-application — against which eight remedial factors are cultivated: faith, aspiration, effort and pliancy against laziness; mindfulness against forgetting the object; introspection against laxity and excitement; application when they are not being quelled; and equanimity when the mind flows calmly.

paraphrase: The mind is settled on the object and settled again, stabilized, brought close, tamed, pacified, fully pacified, made one-pointed and brought into equipoise — the stages of calm abiding as explained by the earlier teachers and by Maitreya.
notes: Stage names read in the local e-text (sthāpayati … ekotīkaroti, samādadhāti); the first four glosses in the paraphrase are from memory.

paraphrase: Neither method without wisdom nor wisdom without method is the bodhisattva's liberation; the perfections of giving and the rest must be joined with the wisdom that understands emptiness, and that wisdom with the method of great compassion.
notes: Summary of the second Bhāvanākrama (Tibetan only); wording from memory.

paraphrase: There is no way other than correct analysis (bhūtapratyavekṣā) by which to achieve non-recollection and non-attention; mere absence of recollection and attention cannot be the cause of non-conceptuality, or one who has fainted would enter it. When the yogin, analysing with correct wisdom, sees no dharma arisen in the three times, he enters non-conceptual wisdom, pacifying all elaboration, penetrates emptiness and is freed from the net of wrong views.
